**Authors:** Emily Holtz  
**Venue:** AERA Open, 2026. DOI: [10.1177/23328584261481430](https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584261481430)  
**Review Date:** 2026-09-25  
**Model:** GPT-6 via Codex  
**Review Mode:** Retrospective (Reader's Guide)

### Overall Assessment: Treat With Caution

Holtz offers a useful exploratory map of Texas one-way dual language (OWDL) and two-way dual language (TWDL) programs, with metropolitan exhibits showing overlapping hot-spot areas in Austin and Houston (Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20). Its contribution is the comparative geographic application of established equity questions, rather than demonstrated effects on access or student outcomes. The published evidence does not securely establish its central claim that TWDL systematically favors affluent, lower-immigrant communities: the principal demographic table is internally incompatible, and the abstract's broad interpretation is not reconciled with the table's qualifications (p. 1; Table 2, p. 10). Enrollment-share clusters and neighborhood demographics also cannot identify who enrolls, who is excluded, or whose linguistic resources benefit others. My overall judgment is treat with caution because the problems affect the central descriptive claim itself, not merely an optional causal interpretation. Use the maps to identify settings and questions for further investigation; await correction or replication before relying on the statewide demographic gradient or the proposed mechanisms.

#### Key Strengths

- The administrative campus records, TEA coordinates, and Census demographics provide a substantive basis for exploratory mapping; joining campus identifiers and geographic identifiers is an appropriate starting point (pp. 5–7; Figure 2, p. 8).
- The paper compares OWDL with TWDL and recognizes OWDL as substantive bilingual provision, avoiding the assumption that absence of TWDL means absence of bilingual education (pp. 22–23).
- The local exhibits retain evidence that complicates a simple separation narrative: Austin and Houston show overlapping program-type hot-spot areas under the local specifications (Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20).
- Named data sources, substantial spatial settings, explicit catchment limitations, and a reported repository and restricted-data request route give readers a meaningful starting point for verification (pp. 5–8, 23–24).

#### Key Concerns

- A document-verifiable incompatibility undermines the main quantitative exhibit. Table 2 says 'Bins reflect county-level American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates' and attributes '69 of 74 statewide hot spots' to El Paso, yet its largest TWDL hot-spot cells are '40 (16.1)' for immigrant density and '25 (18.7)' for income (p. 10, Table 2). Campuses sharing a county must share its bin; these statements cannot all be correct. The document does not identify which component is wrong.
- The exposition overstates a demographic gradient that its own summary qualifies: the abstract says 'TWDL programs cluster in more affluent, lower-immigrant areas' (p. 1), while Table 2 reports 'no consistent statewide association between TWDL hot spot status and either immigrant density or income outside this single county' (p. 10). Program locations and enrollment-share hot spots are different quantities, so this is not a direct like-for-like contradiction; nevertheless, the paper supplies no coherent separate demonstration that reconciles the headline with the qualification. The inconsistent table cannot establish an opposite gradient either.
- My methodological judgment is that the spatial statistics do not establish the claimed allocation processes. Separate nearest-neighbor tests against spatial randomness do not test placement against comparable eligible schools; program-specific hot spots measure relative enrollment-share clustering, not unmet need or admission access. Changing the local samples and distance bands also changes the comparison. Neither nonsignificance nor a cold spot establishes unstable implementation, exclusion, or a temporal process (pp. 7–9, 17–18, 22–23).
- Reconstruction remains incomplete. My sums of Table 2's campus totals are 720 TWDL and 1,091 OWDL for immigrant density, versus 716 and 1,089 for income; the note does not explain those additional differences (p. 10, Table 2). Suppression handling, numerator coverage, demographic matching, and city-subset construction are insufficiently specified in the article (pp. 6–8). The reported deposit may resolve documentation gaps, but its contents and execution were not checked; online supplements and appendices not bound into the PDF were unavailable.
- The literature supplies useful critical framing but needs source checking. Holtz describes Dorner et al. as studying 'school districts in Texas' (p. 3), whereas the source describes data from the 'US Midwest, Southeast, and Texas'; its scope is broader than Holtz's account. The DOI assigned to Morales and Rao (p. 26) leads to a different article by Chris K. Chang-Bacon. These verified defects support selective use of the literature summary, not dismissal of its underlying equity concerns. Sources: [Dorner et al., publisher abstract](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10993-021-09580-6); [SAGE record for the misassigned DOI](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/016146812112300106).

#### What to Rely On

- Reported program sites are geographically uneven in the selected Texas campus sample—Figure 2 (p. 8) supports that descriptive statement, without establishing why sites were chosen or measuring equitable coverage.
- Under the reported local specifications, TWDL and OWDL hot-spot areas overlap in Austin and Houston—this is visible in Figures 10–13 (pp. 18–20), though it does not establish that the programs enroll the same students or offer equal access.
- OWDL provision and exclusion from bilingual education are distinct concepts—the discussion makes this useful distinction (pp. 22–23), without providing comparative evidence of program quality or student benefit.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- The statewide affluent/lower-immigrant TWDL contrast, the inverse OWDL contrast, and exact El Paso concentration counts require verification—the central cross-tabulation cannot be reconciled as labeled (Table 2, p. 10). Treat its county-concentration note as a disputed published statement, not an independently established result.
- Claims about white families' benefits, multilingual learners' exclusion, linguistic-capital extraction, gentrification, or university-driven placement are theoretically informed interpretations—the aggregate cross-sectional data do not observe participants, enrollment decisions, neighborhood change, or learning outcomes (pp. 6–8, 21–24).
- Cross-program or cross-scale hot/cold classifications are not direct comparisons of absolute enrollment shares or access—the analyses use program-specific reference distributions and locally changed spatial neighborhoods (pp. 7–8; Figures 3 and 6, pp. 11 and 14; Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20).
- Policy prescriptions favoring a program model, and claims beyond the selected Texas campuses, need additional evidence—charter and alternative campuses are excluded, the metropolitan cases are purposive, and neither relative effectiveness nor actual family access is measured (pp. 7, 15–16, 23).

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods, writing, and reproducibility reviews identify the same incompatible county-bin/El Paso statements; the rendered Table 2 contains the quoted note and cells (p. 10).
- CONFIRMED — Reproducibility and writing reviews' panel totals match independent addition of Table 2: TWDL 720 versus 716 and OWDL 1,091 versus 1,089; TWDL hot spots sum to 74 versus 73 (p. 10, Table 2).
- CORRECTED — The contribution review recommends citing the El Paso concentration as a finding; that is too strong. Table 2's '69 of 74' attribution cannot coexist with its county-bin cells, so only the existence of the disputed statement is verified (p. 10, Table 2).
- CORRECTED — The methods review's income-majority comparison needs the writing review's qualification: prose says '\$70,000 or greater' (p. 11, discussion of Figure 5, p. 13), but the table uses '\$56–\$70K' and '\$71–\$90K' (p. 10, Table 2); pooled confidence categories also limit comparisons. The table does not substantiate the claim, but does not permit an exact threshold-matched refutation.
- CONFIRMED — The local overlap described across the reviews is visible in the rendered Austin and Houston maps; it concerns hot-spot areas, not identical campus locations or student populations (Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20).
- CONFIRMED — The methods and writing reviews correctly distinguish the operative enrollment-ratio input (p. 8; Table 2, p. 10) from the earlier 'number of students enrolled' wording (p. 6); the synthesis uses the ratio definition.
- CONFIRMED — The literature review's Dorner scope correction and misassigned Morales–Rao DOI were checked against Holtz (pp. 3, 26) and the publisher records linked above; other external literature claims were not adopted without checking.
- COULD NOT CHECK — The reproducibility review accurately reports the Open Practices declaration (p. 24), but the deposit, restricted enrollment records, and executable workflow were not inspected; unbound online supplements and appendices were unavailable.

### Methods Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The administrative-data linkage and spatial mapping provide a useful exploratory description of where dual language programs operate, but the evidence does not securely establish the central claim that TWDL concentrates in affluent, lower-immigrant communities. Internally incompatible reporting in the principal summary table, an inadequate school-location counterfactual, and interpretations of hot-spot classifications as access or exclusion substantially weaken the empirical argument. The weakness is in the support for the published conclusions, not in the choice to conduct a descriptive rather than causal study.

**Strengths:**

- The paper uses credible source types: campus program records requested from the Texas Education Agency, agency campus coordinates, and Census demographic data. Joining campus records by identifier and geographic records by GEOID is an appropriate basis for descriptive mapping, and the paper describes these steps (pp. 5–7).
- Using program enrollment relative to campus enrollment addresses the mechanical relationship between raw enrollment counts and campus size. The paper also reports its coordinate projection, spatial-weight approach, and distance-band procedures, making important analytic choices visible (pp. 7–8; Table 2, p. 10).
- The analysis explicitly considers the background concentration of schools and presents both statewide and locally recalculated maps. The local maps show overlapping TWDL and OWDL concentrations in Austin and Houston, which the findings acknowledge as a complication for the broad sorting interpretation (pp. 16–18; Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20).
- The limitations distinguish the demographic character of program locations from the enrollment experiences of individual families and acknowledge the need for information on attendance boundaries, transfers, and enrollment decisions (p. 23). Those qualifications correctly identify the descriptive scope readers should retain.

**Weaknesses:**

- The main descriptive table is internally incompatible as labeled. Table 2 states that “Bins reflect county-level American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates” and that TWDL hot spots are concentrated in El Paso County, “69 of 74 statewide hot spots, 93%.” Yet the largest TWDL hot-spot entry in any immigrant-density bin is “40 (16.1),” and the largest in any income bin is “25 (18.7)” (p. 10, Table 2). If county characteristics define the bins, all El Paso campuses must occupy the same bin within each panel; neither panel can contain the claimed El Paso count. This is a verifiable incompatibility in the published exhibit, not a dispute about theoretical interpretation. The document does not establish whether the bin geography, counts, or county-concentration statement is wrong.
- The claimed affluent TWDL hot-spot pattern is not supported consistently by the reported summaries. The findings state that “counties with median incomes of \$70,000 or greater represented the majority of hot spot locations” (p. 11, discussion of Figure 5, p. 13). Table 2 instead reports TWDL hot-spot entries of “25 (18.7)” for “\$0–\$40K,” “19 (11.0)” for “\$41–\$55K,” and “16 (12.2)” for “\$56–\$70K,” versus “5 (4.0)” for “\$71–\$90K” and “8 (5.2)” for “\$91K+” (p. 10). Its note also explicitly says there is “no consistent statewide association between TWDL hot spot status and either immigrant density or income outside this single county” (p. 10, Table 2). The table therefore cannot be treated as a coherent quantitative confirmation of the headline statewide gradient; its own internal geography problem also prevents treating it as definitive evidence of the opposite gradient.
- The comparative average nearest-neighbor analysis does not establish the stated program-specific departure from school geography. Separate nearest-neighbor tests against spatial randomness, followed by comparison of their ratios, do not test whether the observed program locations differ from equally sized subsets of eligible existing schools. Population settlement, school grade spans, district program policies, and the distribution of eligible bilingual students can generate the reported clustering without the proposed allocation mechanism (methods, p. 7; clustering findings, p. 9; Figures 1–2, pp. 7–8). No school-location-conditioned reference distribution is reported.
- Getis-Ord Gi* measures neighborhood concentrations of enrollment ratios among included program campuses, not the probability that a local multilingual learner can obtain a program seat. The analysis does not use all eligible students or all eligible campuses as the denominator for need or availability. Total campus enrollment also mixes differences in grade coverage, student composition, program maturity, and capacity with the access construct (pp. 7–8, 14, 23). Foreign-born population share and area household income cannot identify participants’ race, language status, nativity, family resources, or residential catchments. Consequently, the maps do not directly test exclusion, preferential benefits for white families, or extraction of linguistic capital.
- Several interpretations go beyond what the hot-spot statistic establishes. A nonsignificant result is not affirmative evidence of inconsistent implementation or sporadic enrollment, as suggested in the city discussions (pp. 17–18, 22; Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20). Likewise, an El Paso TWDL hot spot and OWDL cold spot do not establish that TWDL has higher proportional enrollment than OWDL: the program-specific analyses use different reference distributions (interpretation, pp. 11–12; Figures 3 and 6, pp. 11 and 14). Local program comparisons additionally use different distance bands. Changing the reference population and spatial scale changes the statistical question, so local-versus-statewide classification differences cannot by themselves identify different mechanisms.
- Uncertainty and sample construction are only partially assessable. The text mentions handling suppressed values without specifying the rules, does not fully reconcile the broader program inventory with the selected analytic campuses, and does not explain all missing demographic classifications (pp. 5–8; Tables 1–2, pp. 5 and 10). It does not report sensitivity to alternative spatial weights, distance bands, or city boundaries, propagation of ACS sampling uncertainty, or whether multiple-testing correction was used for local hot-spot classifications. These omissions matter particularly for exact hot/cold labels and for the regional comparison underlying the argument.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Use the location maps as an exploratory inventory of reported program sites and the hot-spot maps as conditional summaries of spatial enrollment-ratio patterns. Keep presence, enrollment share, unmet need, admission access, and student benefit conceptually separate.
- Do not cite this paper as verified statewide evidence that TWDL high-enrollment clusters favor wealthier, lower-immigrant communities. Before building on that claim, verify the geography and counts in Table 2 against the underlying campus-to-area linkage and reproduce the El Paso concentration statement; the published exhibit cannot reconcile those quantities.
- Treat the observed local overlap in Austin and Houston and the distinct El Paso pattern as hypotheses about regional variation (Figures 10–15, pp. 18–21). Do not interpret the significance labels as comparable measures of program coverage or as direct tests of racialized sorting.
- Give the claims about marketization, gentrification, university influence, and individual exclusion the weight of theoretically informed interpretations. Evidence on changes over time, eligible school and student populations, participant demographics, and enrollment rules would be necessary before those mechanisms could carry policy conclusions. Generalization is limited to the selected Texas campuses and study period; charter and alternative campuses are excluded from the primary analysis (p. 7).

**Detailed Commentary:**

This assessment distinguishes document-verifiable problems from methodological judgment. I read the full article and inspected the tables and map exhibits in the PDF. The incompatible county-bin and El Paso statements in Table 2 are directly verifiable from the published page. My judgment is that they are consequential because this table is the main numerical bridge from the maps to the demographic sorting claim. They cannot be dismissed as a cosmetic inconsistency without first establishing which geography and observations the table actually describes. The underlying data and software execution have not been independently reproduced.

The estimand is also narrower than the argument often implies. A campus enrollment ratio describes the share of its students recorded in a program; a hot-spot statistic describes whether neighboring campuses in the same program-specific dataset have unusually high or low values relative to that dataset. Neither identifies how many nearby students need bilingual services, the number of seats available to them, or the barriers they encounter. The choropleth overlays add contextual descriptions rather than a joint analysis of the relationship between income, immigrant density, urbanicity, and program placement. No multivariable model is inherently required for an exploratory map study, but visual overlays and hot-spot tallies cannot separate these correlated explanations.

The nearest-neighbor comparison is a useful recognition of the background-geography problem, but it does not solve it. To substantiate the published claim that program clustering exceeds what school geography predicts, the reference process would have to condition on plausible school locations and eligibility rather than spatial randomness across the state. Similarly, the broad statewide spatial neighborhood can produce clusters shaped by regional or district organization. Recomputing local analyses is informative, but simultaneously changing the campus sample, reference distribution, and spatial neighborhood is not a controlled robustness check of the same estimand. The selected cities are illustrative cases, not a representative validation sample.

Data quality limits are concrete rather than a reason to distrust administrative data generally. The use of an English Learner program report leaves the precise coverage of the enrollment numerator insufficiently clear for claims about English-dominant beneficiaries. The text does not establish whether all participants or only a reporting subset enter that numerator. The handling of suppressed counts and missing demographic matches also matters for small programs and rural settings. For example, summing the published Table 2 total columns gives TWDL totals of 720 in the immigrant-density panel and 716 in the income panel, and OWDL totals of 1,091 and 1,089, respectively (my arithmetic from p. 10, Table 2). The note identifies geometry exclusions but does not explain these additional between-panel differences. This does not prove consequential selection bias, but it prevents a complete sample audit.

The paper’s explicit catchment and cross-sectional limitations are appropriate, but the conclusion extends beyond them. Page 23 states that the analysis describes neighborhoods where programs are sited, “rather than being a direct measure of student enrollment patterns”; page 24 nevertheless concludes that “the spatial distribution of program type is itself a mechanism of interest convergence.” The former is a defensible statement of what these data measure. The latter requires evidence distinguishing the proposed mechanism from program eligibility, district decisions, demand, staffing, and other explanations. The data do not track neighborhood change, family displacement, participant composition, or benefits received. Excluding charter and alternative schools does not resolve attendance-boundary or transfer-policy problems within the remaining campuses.

The most defensible takeaways are that reported program locations are geographically uneven and that program-specific enrollment-ratio patterns vary by region and analytic scale, including local overlap between program types. Precise demographic gradients, claims about who benefits, and mechanisms of exclusion deserve substantially less weight. The weak rating rests on problems that undermine the central descriptive conclusion itself, rather than on the absence of causal identification. The paper reports a data deposit and restrictions on redistribution of the campus enrollment data (p. 24), but external repository materials and unbound supplements or appendices were not available as part of this review and are not presumed to resolve these problems.

### Literature Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper provides a substantial introduction to critical scholarship on bilingual education, gentrification, and racialized access, but is less dependable as an account of the broader evidence base. Misleading descriptions of cited studies, a demonstrably incorrect reference link, and limited engagement with evidence of benefits for multilingual learners weaken its scholarly positioning; readers should understand its contribution as a Texas spatial application of established arguments rather than a general verdict on who benefits from dual-language education.

**Strengths:**

- The review identifies important intellectual antecedents rather than presenting the critique of dual-language gentrification as new. It explicitly credits Valdés's early cautions, engages Valdez and colleagues on gentrification, and connects more recent qualitative studies of school leadership and exclusion to the Texas question (pp. 2–4). This gives readers useful entry points into the critical bilingual-education literature.
- The framework connects critical race theory, raciolinguistics, and critical spatial analysis, citing Bell, Harris, Flores and Rosa, Soja, and Vélez and Solórzano (pp. 3–5). Its engagement with qualitative scholarship is substantively relevant: decisions about marketing, enrollment, and whose language counts as valuable help explain why program location could matter beyond instructional effectiveness.
- The discussion recognizes that OWDL is a substantive bilingual model rather than simply an inferior substitute for TWDL, and explicitly treats its alignment with multilingual communities as potentially responsive provision (pp. 22–23). This qualification improves the conceptual framing and prevents every difference in program distribution from automatically becoming evidence of deprivation.

**Weaknesses:**

- Descriptions of the geographic and substantive scope of prior research need correction. On p. 3, Holtz introduces studies of Texas and says Dorner et al. studied 'school districts in Texas'; the source actually combines research from the Midwest, Southeast, and Texas. The subsequent description of Chávez-Moreno as examining strategically placed programs appears within the same Texas framing, but the cited article concerns a secondary-program ethnography of racialized policies and practices. Chávez-Moreno's companion publication explicitly locates that larger ethnography in a Midwestern district. These sources support concerns about exclusion, but should not be repeated as independent Texas studies of program siting. Verified against the [Dorner et al. abstract](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10993-021-09580-6), [Chávez-Moreno abstract](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3102/00028312211052508), and the author's [companion study, Context and Methodology](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11256-021-00628-9).
- The closest antecedent to the affluent-location argument receives insufficient attention, and its reference is corrupted. Holtz cites Morales and Rao in passing on p. 3, then on p. 21 positions affluent-area TWDL access as an extension of research about recruitment into working-class immigrant neighborhoods. Yet Morales and Rao's Illinois commentary already argues that dual immersion is disproportionately available in white, middle-class communities. Moreover, the DOI attached to Morales and Rao on p. 26 resolves to a different article by Chris K. Chang-Bacon. The source exists, but the supplied link and journal metadata cannot be trusted as its record. Verified against the publisher's [Morales and Rao commentary](https://journals.sagepub.com/pb-assets/cmscontent/TCZ/Commentaries%20Collection/2015%20Commentaries/How%20Ideology%20and%20Cultural%20Capital%20Shape%20the%20Distribution%20of%20Illinois%E2%80%99%20Bilingual%20Education%20Programs%20-1656522638.pdf) and the [article reached by Holtz's DOI](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/016146812112300106). My judgment is that the novelty is the Texas mapping and explicit program-type comparison, not the proposition that privileged communities can capture access.
- The account of beneficiaries is selective. Although p. 3 acknowledges the equitable aspirations of TWDL and cites Lindholm-Leary and de Jong, the review does not substantively engage modern program-effectiveness evidence. Steele et al.'s lottery study, absent from the paper and references, reports reading benefits and improved English-learner reclassification outcomes. Such evidence does not refute exclusion or gentrification, and its applicant population does not establish equitable access for all families; it does show why access, classroom power, and learning benefits must be evaluated separately. This omission matters because Holtz moves beyond asking where programs exist to broader claims about their beneficiaries and extraction of linguistic resources (pp. 2–4, 22–24). See the [Steele et al. author manuscript, abstract and results](https://jensteele1.github.io/files/2017-dli-effects-preprint.pdf).
- Coverage is incomplete even within the paper's chosen critical tradition. Cervantes-Soon et al.'s review of inequalities in two-way immersion is absent, despite its direct relevance to the discussion of critical consciousness and reimagining programs on p. 23. That synthesis links critiques of unequal opportunity to possibilities for more equitable, integrated bilingual education; it would give readers a fuller account of the alternatives within the field than a contrast organized chiefly around TWDL extraction and OWDL centering. The omission and its relevance are verifiable; its importance to the rating is my judgment. See [Cervantes-Soon et al., abstract](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.3102/0091732X17690120).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite Holtz for its Texas comparison of the geography of TWDL and OWDL, while crediting the earlier gentrification and access arguments to their predecessors. Read Morales and Rao's Illinois commentary alongside the Texas paper to distinguish a new geographic application from a new explanation of unequal access; use the corrected publisher link above.
- Before repeating the Texas literature summary on p. 3, consult Dorner et al. and Chávez-Moreno directly. Keep evidence about school-level policies, racialized participation, and cross-regional qualitative cases separate from evidence about statewide program placement.
- Pair the paper with Steele et al.'s lottery study. The appropriate synthesis is that programs can benefit participating multilingual learners while still distributing access or authority inequitably; neither the achievement study nor Holtz's maps alone answers all parts of the question 'for whom?'. Do not assume that program labels, especially one-way immersion, describe identical populations across states.
- Read Cervantes-Soon et al. for a broader synthesis of equity concerns and critical consciousness within integrated bilingual education. This supplies a scholarly context for the paper's normative recommendations without treating those recommendations as comparative evidence that one program model necessarily serves multilingual learners better.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This assessment covers the complete supplied paper, including its discussion and references. The citation corrections above were checked against publisher records, source abstracts, an author manuscript, and a companion publication by the cited researcher; they are not inferences from citation titles alone. I have not audited every historical claim, obtained every cited full text, or established that the identified omissions exhaust the relevant scholarship. Online supplements and appendices not bound into the supplied PDF were unavailable and were not assumed to contain additional literature engagement.

The paper sits most clearly within critical language policy, sociolinguistics, and the sociology of educational opportunity, with critical geography providing its empirical orientation. That is an appropriate intellectual home for its question. A literature review need not include every adjacent discipline, and the absence of a general developmental-psychology survey is not itself a defect here. The consequential missing bridge is to quantitative policy evaluation: evidence about learning benefits addresses a different dimension of educational advantage from the qualitative evidence about access, recognition, and institutional power.

The weak rating reflects the combined consequences of source-description problems, underdeveloped comparison with a close antecedent, and selective treatment of beneficiaries. It does not imply that the cited critical scholarship is irrelevant or that evidence of positive academic effects disproves racialized exclusion. The strongest reading is that prior qualitative work supplies plausible processes and interpretive questions for the Texas maps. Readers should give less weight to any impression that this literature establishes a universal trajectory from TWDL expansion to displacement, or that the present study independently demonstrates the processes documented in its qualitative predecessors.

### Writing Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper has a usable section structure and informative maps, but its exposition does not reliably reconcile the headline interpretation with the tabulated evidence and later qualifications. Verified inconsistencies in totals, geographic labeling, and the description of hot spots materially impair reader trust; the abstract presents a cleaner affluent-TWDL versus immigrant-community-OWDL contrast than the paper itself sustains.

**Strengths:**

- Organization is easy to follow at the section level: the paper defines TWDL and OWDL, states its research question, separates data from procedures, and proceeds from statewide maps to metropolitan comparisons. Program-specific headings and exhibit references help readers locate the relevant evidence (pp. 1–9, 13–21).
- Table 2 supplies counts as well as within-program, within-bin percentages, and its note defines the enrollment-ratio denominator and the pooling of significance categories (p. 10). The maps use consistent demographic color sequences; the combined metropolitan maps distinguish program types by shape and include legends, scale bars, and north arrows (Figures 10–15, pp. 18–21). These are useful presentation choices even though the table has substantive consistency problems.
- The local-results narrative explicitly acknowledges that Austin and Houston complicate the statewide interpretation, describing overlapping program hot spots rather than concealing this finding (pp. 16–18; Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20). The limitations section clearly explains that campus-neighborhood demographics do not directly measure enrolled students or family enrollment processes (p. 23).

**Weaknesses:**

- Abstract fidelity is poor on the central finding. The abstract states, “TWDL programs cluster in more affluent, lower-immigrant areas” (p. 1), whereas Table 2’s note states that there is “no consistent statewide association between TWDL hot spot status and either immigrant density or income outside this single county” (p. 10). The discussion repeats that qualification (p. 22), and the local results say hot spots “substantially overlap rather than sort into separate territories” (p. 16; Figures 10–11, pp. 18–19). These statements concern somewhat different aspects of clustering, but the abstract does not distinguish them, mention the dominant county, or indicate the local overlap. My judgment is that an abstract-only reader receives an overgeneralized account of both the direction and consistency of the evidence.
- Table 2’s geographic note is internally incompatible with its displayed rows. It says “Bins reflect county-level American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates” and that TWDL hot spots are concentrated in El Paso County, “69 of 74 statewide hot spots” (p. 10). Yet its largest TWDL immigrant-density hot-spot cell is “40 (16.1)” and its largest income hot-spot cell is “25 (18.7)” (Table 2, p. 10). If each county supplies a single demographic value, the reported El Paso hot spots must occupy one bin in each panel; neither panel has a cell large enough. This is a document-verifiable inconsistency, not a disagreement with the theoretical interpretation. The paper does not establish whether the note, the bin geography, or the counts are wrong.
- Published totals require independent reconstruction. The text reports “8,115 bilingual programs” (p. 5), but Table 1’s six rows list “4299,” “5299,” “1226,” “464,” “1351,” and “1226,” which sum to 13,865 campus-program placements (my calculation from Table 1, p. 5). Its note permits multiple programs per school, but that does not reconcile the stated total of programs with the row sum. Separately, summing Table 2 yields 720 TWDL and 1,091 OWDL campuses in the immigrant-density panel, versus 716 and 1,089 in the income panel; hot-spot totals change from 74 to 73 and from 587 to 585, respectively (my calculations from Table 2, p. 10). The geometry-exclusion note does not explain these additional between-panel losses. Readers cannot quote an overall total or denominator without confronting these discrepancies.
- The findings prose does not consistently track the direction of Table 2. It describes the highest-immigrant-density counties as having “the fewest TWDL hot spots” (p. 9; Figures 3–4, pp. 11–12), yet the table’s “36%+” row shows “7 (10.0)” and its “0%–5%” row shows “3 (7.0)” (Table 2, p. 10). Likewise, the claim that “counties with median incomes of \$70,000 or greater represented the majority of hot spot locations” (p. 11; Figure 5, p. 13) is not transparently supported by the income panel: the “\$71–\$90K” and “\$91K+” TWDL hot-spot cells are “5 (4.0)” and “8 (5.2),” whereas the lowest-income cell is “25 (18.7)” (Table 2, p. 10). The prose’s threshold does not exactly match the table’s bin boundary, so the precise majority claim cannot be reconstructed; the displayed pattern nevertheless fails to substantiate the stated affluent-hot-spot contrast. Figure 5 also visually foregrounds El Paso rather than a broad concentration in the darkest income category.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Table 2's rows are not counties. The ICPSR deposit's README (study 308283) states that tract-level income and immigrant density were joined to campuses for the descriptive table, so its "36%+" and "0%–5%" rows are tract bins mislabeled as county bins and do not test the p. 9 sentence about counties; on Figure 4 the 36%+ and 0–5% counties both show no visible TWDL hot spot. The "\$70,000 or greater" comparison in the same paragraph is unaffected. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the ICPSR deposit and the rendered figure.

- The exposition changes what the hot-spot statistic measures. The initial explanation identifies its value as “number of students enrolled in TWDL or OWDL” (p. 6), while the operative procedure specifies “program enrollment divided by total campus enrollment” (p. 8), matching Table 2’s note (p. 10). A reader must privilege the later ratio definition. More consequentially, the claim that nonsignificant campuses imply “sporadic enrollment” (p. 22) gives a temporal meaning to a spatial significance classification. My judgment is that the prose repeatedly blurs program presence, proportional enrollment, spatial significance, and effective community access, although these are different quantities.
- The discussion and conclusion frequently present interpretation as an observed mechanism. The conclusion says program distribution “is itself a mechanism of interest convergence” (p. 24), while the limitations correctly say the analysis documents neighborhoods where programs are sited “rather than being a direct measure of student enrollment patterns” (p. 23). The maps do not show which families enroll, whose capital is extracted, or why programs were placed. A related internal shift concerns El Paso: the local results place “TWDL cold spots” in “proximity to the University of Texas at El Paso” (p. 21; Figures 14–15, pp. 20–21), but the discussion says “the clustering demonstrates that TWDL programs are nearest to the university” (p. 22). Presence near a university is not the same as high-enrollment clustering there; the discussion obscures that distinction when using university proximity to explain the pattern.
- The decisive qualifications are dispersed across Table 2’s small-print note, the local findings, and the late limitations section. Large successive maps separate parts of the argument, and repeated explanations of linguistic capital and interest convergence make the headline interpretation more prominent than its exceptions. Map captions identify overlays but do not independently explain the enrollment denominator or the change from statewide to locally recalculated spatial neighborhoods; readers must return to pp. 7–8. Dense overlapping symbols also make the statewide maps unsuitable for independently verifying exact campus counts (Figures 3–9, pp. 11–17).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Start with the research question on p. 4, the operative procedures on pp. 7–8, Table 2 and its full note on p. 10, and the limitations on p. 23. Then read the abstract again. This sequence makes the measured quantities and scope restrictions visible before the broad interpretation.
- Before quoting a count, percentage, or statewide demographic contrast, check Table 1 against the p. 5 total and reconstruct both panels of Table 2. Treat the county-bin/El Paso incompatibility as unresolved; neither the table nor the prose can be assumed to repair the other.
- For substantive geographic reading, compare the combined statewide map (Figure 9, p. 17) with the paired metropolitan maps (Figures 10–15, pp. 18–21). Read the local recalculation procedure on p. 8 first: local and statewide significance classifications use different spatial contexts and are not interchangeable measures of access.
- A time-constrained reader can skim much of the historical policy narrative and the generic Census/GIS introductions after learning the program definitions and theoretical framing (pp. 2–6). Do not skip the local overlap findings, the Table 2 note, or the enrollment-inference boundary on p. 23. Read extraction, exclusion, and university-driven placement as interpretations requiring evidence beyond these maps.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This assessment concerns fidelity and usability of the published exposition, not the validity of critical race spatial analysis as a framework. I read the complete extracted paper and checked the published PDF images of the central tables and selected statewide and metropolitan maps. The arithmetic discrepancies and quoted changes in wording are directly verifiable within the article; my judgments concern their consequences for comprehension and the strength of the resulting narrative. The table cells generally provide readable within-row denominators, and the maps have useful legends, but those strengths do not resolve the table’s incompatible geography note or the movement between descriptive associations and claims about beneficiaries. Some apparent comparisons also require restraint: Table 2 pools significance categories, whereas parts of the prose describe a particular significance category, so pooled counts alone cannot establish every claimed map–text disagreement. Similarly, a nonsignificant campus is not evidence of no program, and different hot-spot classifications across separately analyzed program types do not by themselves compare their absolute enrollment ratios. The weak rating reflects consequential inconsistencies in the paper’s central message, rather than minor stylistic preferences or an absence of readable sections. No unavailable online supplement or appendix was assumed to resolve these problems.

### Contribution Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper adds a statewide spatial comparison of one-way and two-way dual language programming in Texas, connecting campus program data to neighborhood demographics and examining patterns at regional and metropolitan scales. Its credible contribution is an exploratory account of uneven program geography, including local overlap between program types; its stronger claims that two-way programs systematically favor affluent, low-immigrant communities and extract multilingual learners’ linguistic capital are not established by the published evidence. The question matters, but the gap between these claims and the descriptive results substantially limits the contribution as published.

**Strengths:**

- The distinctive empirical addition, relative to the literature described in the paper, is the joint statewide mapping of OWDL and TWDL using campus administrative records and census demographics, followed by metropolitan analyses (pp. 5–8). This extends the paper’s cited accounts of local program gentrification beyond individual institutional settings; the novelty lies in the comparative evidence and geographic scope, rather than a new theory or spatial method.
- Treating OWDL as substantive bilingual education is a useful conceptual and policy distinction. The discussion explicitly recognizes that OWDL concentration in immigrant communities can represent responsive provision rather than deprivation, and that the availability of dual language relative to English-oriented programs is a separate question (pp. 22–23). Readers therefore gain a more appropriate comparator than a simple TWDL-present/TWDL-absent account of bilingual opportunity.
- The local analyses preserve findings that complicate a simple sorting narrative: Austin and Houston show overlapping TWDL and OWDL hot-spot areas rather than clean separation by program type (pp. 16–18; Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20). My judgment is that this geographic heterogeneity is more informative than the paper’s general claim of affluent-area TWDL concentration.

**Weaknesses:**

- The headline contribution is undermined by the paper’s own summary evidence. The abstract says, “TWDL programs cluster in more affluent, lower-immigrant areas” (p. 1), whereas Table 2’s note states “no consistent statewide association between TWDL hot spot status and either immigrant density or income outside this single county” (p. 10, Table 2). That note attributes 69 of 74 statewide TWDL hot spots to El Paso (p. 10, Table 2). These are verified statements in the document; my judgment is that the evidence supports a geographically concentrated pattern, not the general demographic sorting claim advertised to readers. Program location and enrollment hot spots are distinct quantities, and the paper does not supply a separate systematic demonstration that resolves this gap.
- The analysis measures campus locations and spatial clustering of program enrollment shares, not which students gain access, whose applications are rejected, who benefits educationally, or whether linguistic capital is extracted. Area foreign-born population and household income do not directly identify participating students’ race, language, socioeconomic position, or residence. Consequently, the interest-convergence and raciolinguistic interpretations remain hypotheses informed by prior literature rather than mechanisms established by this study (methods, pp. 6–8; limitations, p. 23).
- The comparison across geographic scales changes the reference population and spatial distance settings as well as the map scale (pp. 7–8). Regional separation alongside metropolitan overlap is potentially informative, but it does not by itself demonstrate that inequity operates through different mechanisms at each level. Likewise, cold spots and nonsignificant spatial statistics do not establish selective exclusion, sporadic enrollment over time, or weak implementation; those interpretations require evidence beyond the mapped enrollment ratios.
- Generalizability is bounded by the Texas program and policy setting, the cross-sectional design, the exclusion of charter and alternative campuses from the primary analyses, and the purposive metropolitan case selection (pp. 5–8, 15–16, 23). The paper honestly acknowledges that campus neighborhoods do not directly measure student enrollment patterns (p. 23), but its conclusion nevertheless describes spatial distribution as “itself a mechanism of interest convergence” (p. 24). My judgment is that this stronger conclusion exceeds the acknowledged scope, including for Texas itself.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite this paper for an exploratory Texas comparison of OWDL and TWDL campus geography and enrollment-share clustering under the reported spatial specifications. When citing the statewide TWDL hot-spot result, include its concentration in El Paso and the lack of a consistent association outside that county reported in Table 2 (p. 10).
- Cite the local maps as evidence that the geographic relationship between program types is heterogeneous: both types occupy overlapping hot-spot areas in Austin and Houston (Figures 10–13, pp. 18–20). Cite the discussion for the conceptual distinction between OWDL provision and exclusion from bilingual education, while keeping that normative interpretation separate from measured program quality (pp. 22–23).
- Do not use the abstract as a reference for a demonstrated statewide affluent/low-immigrant TWDL gradient, or cite the paper as showing that white families displace multilingual learners, that gentrification causes program placement, or that OWDL produces more equitable student outcomes. The published exhibits do not establish the claimed general gradient, and the design does not observe those mechanisms or outcomes.
- Use the maps to identify settings for further investigation rather than to prescribe which program a community should receive. Unresolved questions include how program openings track neighborhood change, how capacity and eligible demand shape enrollment shares, how catchment and transfer rules affect actual participation, and how students are allocated among dual language, transitional bilingual, and ESL options (p. 23). These questions require longitudinal, student-level, or institutional evidence.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The substantive issue is important: geographically uneven access to sustained bilingual instruction can matter for educational opportunity, and distinguishing program models can improve how readers frame that issue. Relative to the prior work as characterized on pp. 2–4, this study contributes broader descriptive coverage and a comparison that includes OWDL rather than another demonstration that marketization is theoretically possible. It is an application of established frameworks and spatial tools, not a methodological innovation or a newly established explanation of program allocation. I cannot rank it as the best available evidence across the full literature from the supplied paper alone; the cited literature was not independently evaluated, and geographic breadth is not equivalent to stronger evidence about access or causal mechanisms.

The appropriate update is that program geography warrants investigation at multiple scales and that metropolitan co-location complicates a simple separation narrative. The inappropriate update is that this study has established statewide racialized extraction through affluent-area TWDL placement. Its central quantitative summary expressly narrows the statewide association, while the enrollment and demographic measures cannot determine beneficiaries or displacement. The limitations discussion is valuable, but those qualifications do not consistently constrain the abstract and conclusion.

The weak rating is a judgment about the contribution as framed and supported, not a judgment that descriptive mapping or a modest contribution to this question lacks value. A bounded descriptive contribution could be adequate; here the paper’s most consequential and quotable claims are substantially stronger than its best-supported findings. Confidence is high in that document-based assessment and lower in any comprehensive ranking of novelty within the field. I read the full supplied paper and inspected the rendered table and selected maps. Online supplements and appendices were unavailable unless bound into the PDF; the repository described on p. 24 was not examined, so no judgment assumes additional analyses or validation there.

### Reproducibility Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper provides named data sources, a public-information-request pathway, substantial spatial-analysis settings, and a reported repository deposit containing preparation code and shareable data. However, undocumented construction decisions and internally incompatible reporting in the central demographic cross-tabulation prevent a reader from verifying the headline spatial-sorting findings as published. The weak rating reflects these consequential verification barriers, not the legitimate restrictions on redistributing campus enrollment data.

**Strengths:**

- Data provenance and an access route are documented: the paper distinguishes the public TEA district report from campus-level information obtained through TEA’s online public information request form, and identifies Census demographic tables and TIGER/Line boundaries (pp. 5–6). This gives a replicator a concrete starting point rather than merely naming an administrative dataset.
- The Open Practices statement supplies a persistent ICPSR deposit identifier, https://doi.org/10.3886/ICPSR308283.V1, and describes public data, merged demographic shapefiles, a Python data-preparation script, and a Data Access File explaining how to request the nonredistributable campus enrollment records (p. 24). These are meaningful transparency commitments; their contents and functionality were not independently verified in this review.
- The main spatial specifications are substantially described: campus-ID joins, coordinate-based campus locations, foreign-born population shares, household-income source, map classification rules, a fixed statewide study area, Euclidean distance, the named Albers projection, enrollment-ratio input, fixed-distance spatial weights, row standardization, and separate locally recalculated city analyses (pp. 6–8). ArcGIS Pro is identified in the methods and versioned in the software reference (pp. 5–6, 25).
- The nearest-neighbor results report ratios, uncertainty statistics, and observed and expected distances in the findings text (p. 9). Table 2 reports campus counts and within-bin percentages, defines its collapsed significance categories, and discloses geometry exclusions (p. 10); map legends present the spatial classifications. These disclosures permit useful document-level checks even without the underlying enrollment data.
- The author identifies where AI assistance entered data preparation and separates that work from the author-executed spatial analyses (pp. 6, 24). The limitations also explicitly distinguish neighborhood demographics around campus locations from students’ actual enrollment pathways (p. 23), helping readers identify which claims the data can directly verify.

**Weaknesses:**

- The central table has an internal geographical incompatibility. Its note states, “Bins reflect county-level American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates (2021)” and “TWDL hot spots are heavily concentrated in El Paso County (69 of 74 statewide hot spots, 93%).” Yet the TWDL hot-spot cells across the immigrant-density bins read “3 (7.0),” “7 (6.7),” “17 (6.7),” “40 (16.1),” and “7 (10.0)” (p. 10, Table 2). Under county-level binning, campuses in the same county must share a bin; none of these bins could contain the reported 69 El Paso hot spots. This is a verifiable inconsistency in the published exhibit, although the document does not establish whether the bins, the geography label, or the El Paso attribution is wrong.
- Table 2’s sample accounting is incomplete. My sums of its displayed totals give 720 TWDL and 1,091 OWDL campuses in the immigrant-density section, versus 716 and 1,089 in the income section; the corresponding TWDL hot-spot sums are 74 and 73 (p. 10, Table 2). The note reports geometry exclusions but does not explain the additional income-section omissions. Thus a replicator cannot identify the complete-case rules or determine whether the demographic comparisons use intentionally different campus samples.
- The central interpretation is not consistently traceable to the reported classifications. The findings describe TWDL “hot spots concentrated in lower-immigrant-density counties” (p. 10, discussion of Figure 4, p. 12), while Table 2’s note says there is “no consistent statewide association between TWDL hot spot status and either immigrant density or income outside this single county” (p. 10). These statements require different evidentiary qualifications, and the paper does not supply a reproducible reconciliation. Regenerating the spatial classifications would therefore not by itself establish the broader interpretation given in the abstract.
- The text identifies cleaning of TEA identifiers and handling of suppressed enrollment values but does not specify the actual rules (p. 6). It also does not identify the exact numerator and denominator source fields, establish whether the program numerator includes all program participants or only reported multilingual learners, or give rules for duplicate records, unmatched campuses, invalid denominators, and missing demographic values. Charter and alternative-campus exclusions are named, but operational flags and an exclusion-by-exclusion sample reconciliation are absent (pp. 5–8). These decisions can change both enrollment ratios and the spatial neighbor set; the reported preparation script may resolve them, but the article alone does not.
- Some consequential GIS choices remain underdocumented despite the extensive settings provided: the geographic boundaries used to extract each city/metro subset, handling of coincident campuses and features without neighbors, the exact campus-to-demographic spatial join, and whether hot-spot classifications incorporate multiple-testing adjustment (pp. 6–8). The published figures do not supply campus identifiers, exact feature-level statistics, or city-specific analytic sample counts, so readers cannot reconstruct the classifications from the maps alone (Figures 3–15, pp. 11–21).
- The deposit description specifically identifies a Python script “used for data preparation,” whereas spatial analyses were executed separately in ArcGIS Pro (pp. 24, 6). The paper does not establish that executable GIS analysis, project settings, or map-generation workflows are included, and does not report the Python dependency environment. This is an unverified limit of the stated replication package, not evidence that the actual deposit lacks those materials.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Begin with the named ICPSR deposit and its Data Access File, then use TEA’s public-information-request pathway for the campus enrollment extract. Check whether the deposit contains executable spatial analyses as well as preparation code, and preserve the exact input vintages and software environments. The repository description should be treated as a reported resource until its files can be inspected and run (pp. 5–6, 24).
- Before relying on the demographic sorting claim, regenerate Table 2 from campus identifiers, coordinates, demographic join keys, enrollment ratios, and hot-spot classifications. Resolve the county-versus-tract binning question, the El Paso attribution, and the unequal demographic-section totals; calculate the county-specific tabulation and repeat the cross-tabulation with El Paso excluded (p. 10, Table 2). Until that reconciliation is available, the published table does not provide a coherent verification target.
- Request or locate the source-field dictionary, suppression rules, join diagnostics, sample-exclusion log, city-subset boundaries, and ArcGIS geoprocessing history. Verify the enrollment numerator’s population before interpreting program-to-campus ratios as access, and compare reconstructed sample membership with the descriptive and analytic populations reported in the paper (pp. 5–8; Table 1, p. 5; Table 2, p. 10).
- Independently regenerate statewide and city-specific spatial classifications using the documented settings, inspect feature-level statistics and neighbor diagnostics, and check sensitivity to geographic subsets and significance adjustment. Keep verified campus-location/enrollment patterns separate from claims about individual beneficiaries, selection, or extraction of linguistic capital: the latter cannot be verified from these aggregate inputs alone, as the paper’s own limitations acknowledge (p. 23).

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a document-based reproducibility assessment following a full reading of the article and visual verification of its tabular exhibits. The restricted campus enrollment data and reported repository package were not inspected or executed; online supplements and appendices were not available for this review, and their contents have not been inferred. Consequently, statements about what the deposit contains are attributed to the Open Practices declaration, while the table arithmetic and incompatible county-bin/El Paso reporting are directly checkable in the supplied PDF.

The strongest part of the reporting is the specification of the intended spatial workflow. This is a descriptive spatial analysis rather than a regression or Bayesian model, so missing priors, sampler diagnostics, or random seeds are not the relevant reproducibility test. The consequential questions are whether the same campus records and enrollment ratios can be rebuilt, whether identical neighborhood definitions generate the same classifications, and whether those classifications reproduce the demographic cross-tabulation and narrative. The article makes substantial progress on the spatial settings but leaves material uncertainty in the first and final links.

My judgment is that these barriers warrant weak rather than adequate reproducibility because the internally incompatible central exhibit leaves even a well-equipped replicator uncertain which published result to reproduce. The explicit source provenance, restricted-access route, reported deposited preparation code, and detailed settings prevent an insufficient rating. A functioning deposit could resolve several documentation gaps, but it would still need to explain the published reporting discrepancies before the headline claim could be treated as independently verified.
